title: Νόστοι τῶν Ἀχαιῶν
titleEn: The Returns of the Achaeans — Odyssey 3.102–209
about: Nestor continues his account of the war's end and the scattered homecomings of the Achaeans: the deaths of Ajax, Achilles, Patroclus and his own son Antilochus; the quarrel between Agamemnon and Menelaus that split the fleet in two; and his own voyage home by way of Tenedos, Lesbos and Euboea. He admits he knows nothing of those who stayed behind, though he has heard how Orestes avenged Agamemnon on Aegisthus, and he urges Telemachus to be brave. Telemachus answers that he wishes the gods had given him the power to punish the suitors' outrages, but admits that no such fortune has been granted to him or his father.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.l: Him then answered the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: Then the Gerenian horseman Nestor answered him:
sentences.n: The reply-formula τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα, ‘him then answered’, opens Nestor's continued speech. Γερήνιος is Nestor's standing epithet; its origin is disputed — either from Gerenia/Gerenon, a place in Messenia, or connected with γέρων ‘old man’ or γέρας ‘honor’. ἱππότα, ‘horseman’, is a nominative in -α, an old form kept for the meter.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλ’, ἐπεί μ’ ἔμνησας ὀιζύος, ἣν ἐν ἐκείνῳ
δήμῳ ἀνέτλημεν μένος ἄσχετοι υἷες Ἀχαιῶν,
sentences.l:
“O friend, since you reminded me of the woe, which in that
land we endured, we sons of the Achaeans unrestrained in fury,
sentences.i: “Friend, since you have reminded me of the suffering we endured in that land — we sons of the Achaeans, whose fury nothing could restrain —
sentences.n: ὦ φίλ’ (for φίλε) is a vocative address. ἔμνησας is aorist of μιμνήσκω ‘remind’, governing the genitive ὀιζύος ‘woe, misery’. ἣν is the relative pronoun ‘which’, not to be confused with the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν. μένος ἄσχετοι, ‘unrestrained in fury’, describes the fixed periphrasis υἷες Ἀχαιῶν, ‘the sons of the Achaeans’.

sentences.t:
ἠμὲν ὅσα ξὺν νηυσὶν ἐπ’ ἠεροειδέα πόντον
πλαζόμενοι κατὰ ληίδ’, ὅπῃ ἄρξειεν Ἀχιλλεύς,
ἠδ’ ὅσα καὶ περὶ ἄστυ μέγα Πριάμοιο ἄνακτος
μαρνάμεθ’·
sentences.l:
both as much as with our ships, over the misty-looking sea
roaming after plunder, wherever Achilles might lead,
and as much as also around the great city of lord Priam
we fought;
sentences.i: both all that we suffered roaming with our ships over the misty sea after plunder, wherever Achilles led, and all that we suffered fighting around the great city of lord Priam;
sentences.n: ἠμὲν … ἠδ(ὲ) is a correlative ‘both … and’, here spread over four lines. ἐπ’ ἠεροειδέα πόντον is the fixed phrase ‘over the misty-looking sea’. ὅπῃ ἄρξειεν is an optative of general past time, ‘wherever Achilles happened to lead’. Πριάμοιο is a genitive in -οιο (Attic -ου).

sentences.t: ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειτα κατέκταθεν ὅσσοι ἄριστοι.
sentences.l: there then thereafter were slain as many as were best.
sentences.i: there, one after another, all the best of us were killed.
sentences.n: κατέκταθεν is an augmented aorist passive (root aorist in -θεν) of κατακτείνω ‘kill’, 3rd pl.: the preverb κατά elides its final vowel before the augment (κατ’ + ἔκταθεν), which is what shows the augment is present; the unaugmented form is κτάθεν, found elsewhere in Homer. ὅσσοι ἄριστοι, ‘as many as were best’, sets up the roll-call of the dead that follows.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα μὲν Αἴας κεῖται ἀρήιος, ἔνθα δ’ Ἀχιλλεύς,
ἔνθα δὲ Πάτροκλος, θεόφιν μήστωρ ἀτάλαντος,
ἔνθα δ’ ἐμὸς φίλος υἱός, ἅμα κρατερὸς καὶ ἀμύμων,
Ἀντίλοχος, πέρι μὲν θείειν ταχὺς ἠδὲ μαχητής·
sentences.l:
There lies warlike Ajax, there Achilles,
there Patroclus, a counselor equal to the gods,
there my own dear son, at once mighty and blameless,
Antilochus, exceedingly swift to run and a fighter;
sentences.i: There lies warlike Ajax, there Achilles, there Patroclus, a counselor the equal of the gods, and there my own dear son Antilochus, mighty and blameless at once, outstandingly swift of foot and a fighter;
sentences.n: ἀρήιος ‘warlike’ (of Ares) is new to this part and recurs at 167. θεόφιν is a dative/instrumental plural in -φι, ‘by the gods’ measure’. ἀμύμων keeps the table's fixed ‘blameless’. Antilochus, Nestor's son, died at Troy defending his father from a Trojan spear.

sentences.t: ἄλλα τε πόλλ’ ἐπὶ τοῖς πάθομεν κακά·
sentences.l: and many other evils besides these we suffered;
sentences.i: and we suffered many other troubles besides;
sentences.n: πάθομεν is an unaugmented aorist (Attic ἐπάθομεν). τοῖς, ‘besides these things’, resumes the losses just named. κακά here is the plain noun ‘evils, troubles’, distinct from the epithet ἀτάσθαλα at 207.

sentences.t:
τίς κεν ἐκεῖνα
πάντα γε μυθήσαιτο καταθνητῶν ἀνθρώπων;
sentences.l:
who could those things,
all of them, tell of, of mortal men?
sentences.i: what mortal man could tell the whole of it?
sentences.n: κεν with the optative μυθήσαιτο makes a potential question, ‘who could tell’. καταθνητῶν ἀνθρώπων is a partitive genitive with τίς, ‘which of mortal men’ — that is, no one. The rhetorical question closes Nestor's list of the dead.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ εἰ πεντάετές γε καὶ ἑξάετες παραμίμνων
ἐξερέοις ὅσα κεῖθι πάθον κακὰ δῖοι Ἀχαιοί·
sentences.l:
Not even if for five years, yes, and six years, remaining
you should ask out all the evils that there suffered the heavenly Achaeans;
sentences.i: Not even if you stayed on here for five years, or six, asking about all the woes the heavenly Achaeans suffered there;
sentences.n: παραμίμνων, ‘remaining beside’, is a participle attached to the unexpressed subject of ἐξερέοις, a future-toned optative of ἐξερέω ‘inquire closely, ask out’, inside the εἰ-clause. δῖοι Ἀχαιοί applies the table's fixed ‘heavenly’ (elsewhere of Odysseus) to the Achaeans generally, an ordinary Homeric extension of δῖος.

sentences.t: πρίν κεν ἀνιηθεὶς σὴν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἵκοιο.
sentences.l: sooner, wearied, to your fatherland you would come.
sentences.i: you would grow weary and reach your own native land before I had finished.
sentences.n: πρίν κεν … ἵκοιο, ‘before you would come’, answers the εἰ-clause of the line before: you would tire and go home before Nestor's tale was told. ἀνιηθείς is the aorist passive participle of ἀνιάω ‘vex, weary’.

sentences.t:
εἰνάετες γάρ σφιν κακὰ ῥάπτομεν ἀμφιέποντες
παντοίοισι δόλοισι, μόγις δ’ ἐτέλεσσε Κρονίων.
sentences.l:
for nine years for them evils we wove, busying ourselves
with all manner of stratagems, and scarcely did the son of Cronus bring it to pass.
sentences.i: For nine years we wove evils for them, busy with every kind of stratagem, and the son of Cronus barely brought it to an end.
sentences.n: ῥάπτομεν, literally ‘stitch, weave’, is used of contriving harm, much as English says ‘weave a plot’. σφιν, ‘for them’, refers to the Trojans. Κρονίων ‘son of Cronus’ is Zeus; μόγις ‘scarcely, with effort’ marks how long the war dragged on even under his will.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ οὔ τίς ποτε μῆτιν ὁμοιωθήμεναι ἄντην
ἤθελ’, ἐπεὶ μάλα πολλὸν ἐνίκα δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
παντοίοισι δόλοισι, πατὴρ τεός, εἰ ἐτεόν γε
κείνου ἔκγονός ἐσσι·
sentences.l:
There no one ever in cunning to be made equal face to face
wished, since by very much surpassed heavenly Odysseus
in all manner of stratagems, your father, if indeed
of that man's stock you are;
sentences.i: There, no one ever wished to be matched face to face in cunning with your father, heavenly Odysseus, since he far surpassed all others in every kind of stratagem — if indeed you truly are his offspring;
sentences.n: μῆτιν ὁμοιωθήμεναι, ‘to be made equal in cunning’, is a complementary infinitive after ἤθελ(ε) ‘wished’, not a purpose infinitive: ἐθέλω regularly takes its infinitive as a direct object. ὁμοιωθήμεναι is an aorist passive infinitive in the epic ending -ήμεναι. δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς keeps the table's ‘heavenly Odysseus’. εἰ ἐτεόν γε, ‘if indeed truly’, is a polite proviso, not real doubt.

sentences.t: σέβας μ’ ἔχει εἰσορόωντα.
sentences.l: awe holds me, looking on you.
sentences.i: Awe takes hold of me as I look at you.
sentences.n: σέβας, ‘awe, reverent wonder’, is the subject of ἔχει, ‘holds me’. εἰσορόωντα, an uncontracted present participle, agrees with the implied ‘me’: ‘as I gaze on you’. Nestor marvels at how closely Telemachus's speech resembles his father's.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι γὰρ μῦθοί γε ἐοικότες, οὐδέ κε φαίης
ἄνδρα νεώτερον ὧδε ἐοικότα μυθήσασθαι.
sentences.l:
For indeed your words at least are fitting, nor would you say
a younger man so fittingly could speak.
sentences.i: Your words at least are fitting, and you would not think a younger man could speak so fittingly.
sentences.n: ἐοικότες, ‘fitting, resembling’, is a perfect participle used adjectivally, echoed twice in these two lines. οὐδέ κε φαίης, ‘nor would you say’, is a potential optative, a common idiom of polite understatement. νεώτερον, ‘younger’, implies youth not usually equal to such wise speech.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἦ τοι ἧος μὲν ἐγὼ καὶ δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
οὔτε ποτ’ εἰν ἀγορῇ δίχ’ ἐβάζομεν οὔτ’ ἐνὶ βουλῇ,
ἀλλ’ ἕνα θυμὸν ἔχοντε νόῳ καὶ ἐπίφρονι βουλῇ
φραζόμεθ’ Ἀργείοισιν ὅπως ὄχ’ ἄριστα γένοιτο.
sentences.l:
There then, indeed, as long as I and heavenly Odysseus
neither ever in the assembly spoke apart nor in council,
but having one mind in thought and in prudent counsel
we devised for the Argives how things might turn out best by far.
sentences.i: In those days, so long as heavenly Odysseus and I never spoke at odds either in the assembly or in council, but shared a single mind, and with sound judgment and wise counsel worked out for the Argives how everything might turn out best,
sentences.n: ἧος, ‘as long as’, opens a temporal clause spanning the sentence. δίχ’ ἐβάζομεν, ‘spoke apart, disagreed’, is answered by ἀλλ’ ἕνα θυμὸν ἔχοντε, a dual participle: ‘the two of us having one mind’. Ἀργείοισιν, dative plural in -οισι(ν), is another name for the Achaeans.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Πριάμοιο πόλιν διεπέρσαμεν αἰπήν,
βῆμεν δ’ ἐν νήεσσι, θεὸς δ’ ἐκέδασσεν Ἀχαιούς,
sentences.l:
but when Priam's city we had utterly sacked, the steep one,
and we went aboard the ships, and a god scattered the Achaeans,
sentences.i: But when we had utterly sacked Priam's steep city, and had gone aboard our ships, and a god scattered the Achaeans,
sentences.n: διεπέρσαμεν, ‘sacked utterly’, carries the intensive prefix δια-. αἰπήν, ‘steep’, describes Troy's height, distinct from the fixed phrase αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος. βῆμεν is an unaugmented aorist of βαίνω. θεός, left unnamed, is Homer's common way of letting a god act without naming which one.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότε δὴ Ζεὺς λυγρὸν ἐνὶ φρεσὶ μήδετο νόστον
Ἀργείοις, ἐπεὶ οὔ τι νοήμονες οὐδὲ δίκαιοι
πάντες ἔσαν·
sentences.i: then it was that Zeus began devising in his heart a grievous return for the Argives, since not all of them had been sensible or just,
sentences.n: λυγρὸν … νόστον, ‘grievous return’, is new to this part; the adjective λυγρός recurs at 194, there describing Aegisthus's crime (λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον, ‘grievous destruction’) rather than the same noun. λυγρός is a stock word for ‘baneful, miserable’. νοήμονες and δίκαιοι are predicate adjectives with ἔσαν (Attic ἦσαν); the enjambed πάντες ἔσαν holds the negation open across the line-break.

sentences.t:
τῶ σφεων πολέες κακὸν οἶτον ἐπέσπον
μήνιος ἐξ ὀλοῆς γλαυκώπιδος ὀβριμοπάτρης.
sentences.l:
wherefore of them many an evil doom met
from the deadly wrath of the gleaming-eyed, mighty-fathered one.
sentences.i: and so many of them met an evil fate, through the deadly wrath of the gleaming-eyed goddess, she of the mighty father.
sentences.n: τῶ, ‘wherefore’, is a demonstrative used as a connective. ἐπέσπον is aorist of ἐφέπω, ‘met with, followed upon’. γλαυκώπιδος ὀβριμοπάτρης combines two fixed epithets for Athena, ‘gleaming-eyed’ and ‘she of the mighty father’, without naming her — the periphrasis is kept literal rather than resolved to her name.

sentences.t: ἥ τ’ ἔριν Ἀτρεΐδῃσι μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν ἔθηκε.
sentences.l: who indeed strife among the sons of Atreus, between the two of them, set.
sentences.i: for she set strife between the two sons of Atreus.
sentences.n: ἥ refers back to Athena. Ἀτρεΐδῃσι, a dative plural in -ῃσι, is ‘for/among the sons of Atreus’ — Agamemnon and Menelaus, a title that recurs through this part. μετ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν, ‘between the two of them’, stresses that the quarrel struck both brothers.

sentences.t:
τὼ δὲ καλεσσαμένω ἀγορὴν ἐς πάντας Ἀχαιούς,
μάψ, ἀτὰρ οὐ κατὰ κόσμον, ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα,
οἱ δ’ ἦλθον οἴνῳ βεβαρηότες υἷες Ἀχαιῶν,
μῦθον μυθείσθην, τοῦ εἵνεκα λαὸν ἄγειραν.
sentences.l:
and the two, having called an assembly for all the Achaeans,
rashly, and not in order, at the sun's going down,
and they came, heavy with wine, the sons of the Achaeans,
the two told the matter for the sake of which they had gathered the people.
sentences.i: The two of them called all the Achaeans to assembly, rashly and out of due order, at sunset, and the sons of the Achaeans came heavy with wine, and the two brothers set out the matter for which they had gathered the people.
sentences.n: καλεσσαμένω and μυθείσθην are dual forms, since Agamemnon and Menelaus act as a pair. μάψ, ‘rashly, without cause’, and οὐ κατὰ κόσμον, ‘not in due order’, condemn calling an assembly at sundown, an unheard-of hour. βεβαρηότες, a perfect participle, ‘weighed down’, shows the men have been drinking.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἦ τοι Μενέλαος ἀνώγει πάντας Ἀχαιοὺς
νόστου μιμνήσκεσθαι ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης,
οὐδ’ Ἀγαμέμνονι πάμπαν ἑήνδανε·
sentences.i: Then Menelaus urged all the Achaeans to think of their homecoming over the sea's broad back, but this did not please Agamemnon at all;
sentences.n: ἀνώγει, ‘urged, bade’, governs the infinitive μιμνήσκεσθαι with the genitive νόστου. ἐπ’ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης, ‘over the broad back of the sea’, pictures the sea as a great animal's spine. ἑήνδανε is an augmented imperfect of ἁνδάνω ‘please’ (the root once began with digamma, ϝανδάνω, so the augment ἐ- shows here as ἑ-, as in the related ἥνδανε of Iliad 1.24), with the dative Ἀγαμέμνονι; the unaugmented form ἄνδανε is also found in Homer.

sentences.t:
βούλετο γάρ ῥα
λαὸν ἐρυκακέειν ῥέξαι θ’ ἱερὰς ἑκατόμβας,
ὡς τὸν Ἀθηναίης δεινὸν χόλον ἐξακέσαιτο,
νήπιος, οὐδὲ τὸ ᾔδη, ὃ οὐ πείσεσθαι ἔμελλεν·
sentences.i: for he wished to hold the army back and offer sacred hecatombs, so as to appease Athena's dread anger — the fool, for he did not know that she was not to be won over;
sentences.n: ἐρυκακέειν and ῥέξαι are complementary infinitives after βούλετο. ἑκατόμβη, ‘hecatomb’, an offering of a hundred oxen, was the largest sacrifice a Greek could make. νήπιος, ‘fool, child’, is the narrator's own judgment, dropped in mid-sentence. πείσεσθαι, future infinitive of πείθω, here means ‘be persuaded, won over’.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ τ’ αἶψα θεῶν τρέπεται νόος αἰὲν ἐόντων.
sentences.l: for not quickly is the mind of the gods who are forever turned.
sentences.i: for the mind of the gods who are forever is not quickly changed.
sentences.n: θεῶν … αἰὲν ἐόντων keeps the table's fixed ‘the gods who are forever’. τρέπεται, ‘is turned, changed’, together with the negative and αἶψα ‘quickly’, states a general truth; the epic τε in γάρ τ(ε) marks it as such.

sentences.t:
ὣς τὼ μὲν χαλεποῖσιν ἀμειβομένω ἐπέεσσιν
ἕστασαν·
sentences.l:
So the two, with harsh words answering one another,
stood;
sentences.i: So the two of them stood there, exchanging harsh words,
sentences.n: τὼ … ἀμειβομένω is another dual form, ‘the two of them answering’. χαλεποῖσιν ἐπέεσσιν, ‘with harsh words’, is a dative of means. ἕστασαν, a pluperfect-form verb used with imperfect sense, means ‘they stood, were standing’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἀνόρουσαν ἐυκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοὶ
ἠχῇ θεσπεσίῃ, δίχα δέ σφισιν ἥνδανε βουλή.
sentences.l:
and they sprang up, the well-greaved Achaeans,
with a wondrous outcry, and their counsel pleased them in two ways.
sentences.i: while the well-greaved Achaeans sprang up with a wondrous clamor, their counsel divided between the two sides.
sentences.n: ἐυκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί keeps the table's fixed ‘well-greaved Achaeans’. θεσπεσίῃ, ‘wondrous, prodigious’, echoes θεσπέσιος already fixed elsewhere in this table; here it describes the crowd's noise. δίχα … ἥνδανε βουλή, literally ‘counsel pleased them split in two’, means they split into two camps.

sentences.t:
νύκτα μὲν ἀέσαμεν χαλεπὰ φρεσὶν ὁρμαίνοντες
ἀλλήλοις·
sentences.l:
The night we passed, harsh things in our hearts pondering
against one another;
sentences.i: We spent the night brooding harsh thoughts against one another,
sentences.n: ἀέσαμεν is an aorist meaning ‘pass the night’, from a root distinct from ἄημι ‘blow’. φρεσὶν ὁρμαίνοντες, ‘pondering in our hearts’, takes the dative ἀλλήλοις, ‘against one another’: the two war-parties brooding with mutual resentment.

sentences.t: ἐπὶ γὰρ Ζεὺς ἤρτυε πῆμα κακοῖο·
sentences.l: for Zeus was contriving upon us woe of evil;
sentences.i: for Zeus was preparing suffering upon suffering for us;
sentences.n: ἐπὶ … ἤρτυε is tmesis, ‘was fitting/preparing upon [us]’, from ἐπαρτύω. πῆμα κακοῖο, literally ‘woe of evil’, is an intensifying genitive, ‘woe upon woe’.

sentences.t:
ἠῶθεν δ’ οἱ μὲν νέας ἕλκομεν εἰς ἅλα δῖαν
κτήματά τ’ ἐντιθέμεσθα βαθυζώνους τε γυναῖκας.
sentences.l:
At dawn some of us drew our ships down into the heavenly brine
and put aboard our goods and the deep-girdled women.
sentences.i: At dawn some of us drew our ships down to the bright salt sea and loaded our goods and the deep-girdled women aboard.
sentences.n: ἠῶθεν, ‘from dawn, at daybreak’, carries the directional suffix -θεν. ἅλα δῖαν, ‘the heavenly brine’, applies the table's fixed ‘heavenly’ to the sea. βαθυζώνους, ‘deep-girdled’, a stock epithet for women describing the long girdled robe; the women here are captives taken as spoil.

sentences.t:
ἡμίσεες δ’ ἄρα λαοὶ ἐρητύοντο μένοντες
αὖθι παρ’ Ἀτρεΐδῃ Ἀγαμέμνονι, ποιμένι λαῶν·
sentences.l:
but half the people, then, were held back, remaining
there beside Atreus' son Agamemnon, shepherd of the people;
sentences.i: but half the army was held back, remaining there with Atreus' son Agamemnon, shepherd of the people;
sentences.n: ἡμίσεες, ‘half’, splits the army into the two parties named through the rest of the passage. ἐρητύοντο is an unaugmented imperfect passive, ‘were held back, restrained’. ποιμένι λαῶν, ‘shepherd of the people’, is a common title for a king, picturing him as guardian of his flock.

sentences.t: ἡμίσεες δ’ ἀναβάντες ἐλαύνομεν·
sentences.l: but half, having gone aboard, we rowed onward;
sentences.i: while the rest of us went aboard and rowed off;
sentences.n: ἀναβάντες, ‘having gone up, embarked’, is an aorist participle. ἐλαύνομεν, ‘we drove, rowed’, shifts into the first person: Nestor was among this half of the fleet.

sentences.t:
αἱ δὲ μάλ’ ὦκα
ἔπλεον, ἐστόρεσεν δὲ θεὸς μεγακήτεα πόντον.
sentences.l:
and the ships very swiftly
sailed on, and a god spread smooth the vast-yawning sea.
sentences.i: and the ships sailed on very swiftly, and a god smoothed the vast, gaping sea for us.
sentences.n: αἱ, ‘the ships’ (νῆες), is understood from context. ἐστόρεσεν, ‘spread smooth, calmed’, is aorist of στόρνυμι. μεγακήτεα, ‘vast, monster-holding’, is built on κῆτος ‘sea-monster’, picturing the deep sea as home to great creatures.

sentences.t:
ἐς Τένεδον δ’ ἐλθόντες ἐρέξαμεν ἱρὰ θεοῖσιν,
οἴκαδε ἱέμενοι·
sentences.l:
and to Tenedos having come we offered sacrifices to the gods,
longing for home;
sentences.i: and when we reached Tenedos, we offered sacrifices to the gods, eager for home;
sentences.n: Τένεδος, Tenedos, is a small island off the Troad, the fleet's first stop homeward. ἱρά (Attic ἱερά) is neuter plural, ‘sacred things, offerings’. ἱέμενοι, ‘longing, straining forward’, is the same participle used of Odysseus in the poem's opening lines.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς δ’ οὔ πω μήδετο νόστον,
σχέτλιος, ὅς ῥ’ ἔριν ὦρσε κακὴν ἔπι δεύτερον αὖτις.
sentences.l:
but Zeus not yet was devising our return,
cruel one, who then stirred up evil strife a second time again.
sentences.i: but Zeus was not yet planning our return — the cruel god, who stirred up bitter strife a second time.
sentences.n: σχέτλιος, ‘cruel, merciless’, is applied directly to Zeus here, a striking judgment for a god to receive. ἔπι δεύτερον αὖτις piles up three words for repetition, ‘a second time, again, once more’, stressing that the leaders' quarrel flared up twice.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἀποστρέψαντες ἔβαν νέας ἀμφιελίσσας
ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆα ἄνακτα δαΐφρονα, ποικιλομήτην,
αὖτις ἐπ’ Ἀτρεΐδῃ Ἀγαμέμνονι ἦρα φέροντες·
sentences.i: Some turned their curved ships back and went with lord Odysseus, wise-hearted and full of shifting cunning, once more to please Atreus' son Agamemnon;
sentences.n: ἀμφιελίσσας, ‘curved at both ends’, is a standing epithet of ships. δαΐφρων is one of the table's three kept-distinct epithets of Odysseus, ‘wise-minded’ (the root δαῆναι ‘to learn’ is followed in both layers, though disputed). ποικιλομήτην, ‘of shifting, many-colored cunning’, is transparent, built on μῆτις. ἦρα φέροντες is an idiom, ‘bringing favor, currying favor’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ σὺν νηυσὶν ἀολλέσιν, αἵ μοι ἕποντο,
φεῦγον, ἐπεὶ γίγνωσκον, ὃ δὴ κακὰ μήδετο δαίμων.
sentences.l:
But I with my ships gathered together, which followed me,
fled, since I knew that indeed evils a god was devising.
sentences.i: But I fled with the ships that followed me, all together, since I could tell that a god was planning evil.
sentences.n: ἀολλέσιν, ‘gathered, all together’, describes Nestor's own squadron keeping formation. γίγνωσκον is an unaugmented imperfect, ‘I perceived, could tell’. δαίμων, ‘a god, a divine power’, is left unspecified, Nestor's instinct that trouble was brewing.

sentences.t: φεῦγε δὲ Τυδέος υἱὸς ἀρήιος, ὦρσε δ’ ἑταίρους.
sentences.l: and fled the son of Tydeus, warlike, and he roused his companions.
sentences.i: The warlike son of Tydeus fled too, and roused his companions to follow.
sentences.n: Τυδέος υἱός, ‘the son of Tydeus’, is a periphrasis for Diomedes, used here instead of his name; the patronymic Τυδεΐδης names him directly at 181. ἀρήιος, ‘warlike’, recurs from 109. ὦρσε is aorist of ὄρνυμι, ‘roused, stirred up’.

sentences.t:
ὀψὲ δὲ δὴ μετὰ νῶι κίε ξανθὸς Μενέλαος,
ἐν Λέσβῳ δ’ ἔκιχεν δολιχὸν πλόον ὁρμαίνοντας,
sentences.l:
and late indeed after the two of us came fair-haired Menelaus,
and at Lesbos he overtook us pondering a long voyage,
sentences.i: Fair-haired Menelaus came after us late, and caught up with us at Lesbos as we debated the long crossing,
sentences.n: μετὰ νῶι, ‘after the two of us’, is dual, since Nestor and Diomedes had sailed on together. ξανθὸς Μενέλαος keeps the table's fixed ‘fair-haired Menelaus’. δολιχὸν πλόον ὁρμαίνοντας, ‘pondering a long voyage’, sets up the indirect question that follows.

sentences.t:
ἢ καθύπερθε Χίοιο νεοίμεθα παιπαλοέσσης,
νήσου ἔπι Ψυρίης, αὐτὴν ἐπ’ ἀριστέρ’ ἔχοντες,
ἦ ὑπένερθε Χίοιο, παρ’ ἠνεμόεντα Μίμαντα.
sentences.l:
whether above rugged Chios we should go,
toward the island of Psyria, keeping it itself on our left,
or below Chios, past windy Mimas.
sentences.i: whether we should sail above rugged Chios, toward the island of Psyria, keeping it on our left, or below Chios, past windy Mimas.
sentences.n: νεοίμεθα is an optative in an indirect deliberative question, ‘whether we should go’. παιπαλοέσσης, ‘rugged, craggy’, describes Chios' terrain. Psyria and Mimas, a headland opposite Chios, are minor Aegean landmarks marking the two possible routes home.

sentences.t: ᾐτέομεν δὲ θεὸν φῆναι τέρας·
sentences.l: and we asked the god to show a sign;
sentences.i: We asked the god to show us a sign;
sentences.n: ᾐτέομεν is an augmented imperfect of αἰτέω, ‘ask, request’, with its ending left uncontracted: the diphthong αι- lengthens under the augment to ᾐ- (the unaugmented form would keep αἰτέομεν with the diphthong unchanged), while the ending -εομεν stays open rather than contracting to Attic -οῦμεν. φῆναι is the aorist infinitive of φαίνω, ‘show, reveal’. τέρας, ‘a sign, portent’, is the standard word for a divine omen sought before a risky crossing.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἡμῖν
δεῖξε, καὶ ἠνώγει πέλαγος μέσον εἰς Ἐύβοιαν
τέμνειν, ὄφρα τάχιστα ὑπὲκ κακότητα φύγοιμεν.
sentences.l:
and he to us
showed one, and bade us the open sea through the middle to Euboea
cut across, that most quickly out from under misery we might flee.
sentences.i: and he showed us one, and told us to cut straight across the open sea to Euboea, so that we might escape our troubles as quickly as possible.
sentences.n: ὅ γε, ‘he’, refers to the unnamed god. ἠνώγει, ‘bade, commanded’, governs the infinitive τέμνειν, ‘to cut’, itself governing πέλαγος μέσον, ‘the open sea through the middle’, i.e. the most direct crossing. ὑπὲκ κακότητα φύγοιμεν, ‘flee out from under trouble’, is an optative of purpose after ὄφρα.

sentences.t: ὦρτο δ’ ἐπὶ λιγὺς οὖρος ἀήμεναι·
sentences.l: and there arose upon us a clear-sounding wind to blow;
sentences.i: A clear, fresh wind sprang up to carry us on;
sentences.n: ὦρτο is aorist of ὄρνυμι, ‘arose’. λιγύς, ‘clear, shrill’, usually describes voices or instruments but here a keen, whistling wind. ἀήμεναι, an epic infinitive in -μεναι (Attic ἀῆναι), ‘to blow’, is epexegetic with οὖρος.

sentences.t:
αἱ δὲ μάλ’ ὦκα
ἰχθυόεντα κέλευθα διέδραμον, ἐς δὲ Γεραιστὸν
ἐννύχιαι κατάγοντο·
sentences.i: and the ships sped very swiftly over the fish-filled sea-paths, and put in at Geraestus by night;
sentences.n: ἰχθυόεντα κέλευθα, ‘fish-filled paths’, echoes the table's fixed ‘the watery ways’ (3.71), a poetic name for the sea's ways. Geraestus is a headland at the southern tip of Euboea. ἐννύχιαι, ‘by night’, and κατάγοντο, ‘put in to land’, describe a landing made in darkness.

sentences.t:
Ποσειδάωνι δὲ ταύρων
πόλλ’ ἐπὶ μῆρ’ ἔθεμεν, πέλαγος μέγα μετρήσαντες.
sentences.l:
and to Poseidon of bulls
many thighs we laid upon the altar, having measured the great open sea.
sentences.i: and to Poseidon we laid many bulls' thighs on the altar-fire, having crossed the great open sea.
sentences.n: Ποσειδάωνι echoes the table's fixed ‘to Poseidon the lord’, here without the title ἄνακτι. μῆρα, ‘thigh-pieces’, wrapped in fat, were the god's portion burned in sacrifice. μετρήσαντες, ‘having measured’, is used of a sea-crossing as if pacing out a distance.

sentences.t:
τέτρατον ἦμαρ ἔην, ὅτ’ ἐν Ἄργεϊ νῆας ἐίσας
Τυδεΐδεω ἕταροι Διομήδεος ἱπποδάμοιο
ἵστασαν·
sentences.i: It was the fourth day when the companions of Tydeus' son, horse-taming Diomedes, moored their well-balanced ships at Argos;
sentences.n: νῆας ἐίσας keeps the table's fixed ‘well-balanced ships’ (the sense of ἐίση itself is uncertain, as noted there). Τυδεΐδεω, ‘son of Tydeus’, is the patronymic form of the periphrasis used at 167 for Diomedes. ἱπποδάμοιο, ‘horse-taming’, is the epithet the table fixes for Nestor, here applied to Diomedes.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγώ γε Πύλονδ’ ἔχον, οὐδέ ποτ’ ἔσβη
οὖρος, ἐπεὶ δὴ πρῶτα θεὸς προέηκεν ἀῆναι.
sentences.l:
but I, for my part, held my course for Pylos, nor ever died out
the wind, since first of all a god had sent it forth to blow.
sentences.i: but I held my course for Pylos, and the wind never once died, since the god had first sent it blowing on its way.
sentences.n: Πύλονδ(ε), ‘to Pylos’, carries the directional suffix -δε. ἔσβη is an augmented root aorist of σβέννυμι, ‘be quenched, die out’ (the augment ἐ- is prefixed to the consonant-initial root σβη-; the unaugmented form would be the bare σβη), here of the wind rather than fire. προέηκεν, ‘sent forth’, is aorist of προΐημι: the same fair wind carried Nestor all the way home.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἦλθον, φίλε τέκνον, ἀπευθής, οὐδέ τι οἶδα
κείνων, οἵ τ’ ἐσάωθεν Ἀχαιῶν οἵ τ’ ἀπόλοντο.
sentences.l:
So I came, dear child, without learning, nor do I know anything
of those, both who were saved of the Achaeans and who perished.
sentences.i: So I came home, dear child, without word, and I know nothing of those Achaeans, which were saved and which were lost.
sentences.n: ἀπευθής, ‘without tidings, uninformed’, marks Nestor's ignorance on arrival: he sailed home too fast to learn the others' fates. φίλε τέκνον, ‘dear child’, is his affectionate address to Telemachus. οἵ τ’ … οἵ τ(ε), ‘both who … and who’, covers both outcomes, survival and death.

sentences.t:
ὅσσα δ’ ἐνὶ μεγάροισι καθήμενος ἡμετέροισι
πεύθομαι, ἣ θέμις ἐστί, δαήσεαι, οὐδέ σε κεύσω.
sentences.l:
but as much as, sitting in our halls,
I learn by hearsay, as is right, you shall be told, nor will I hide it from you.
sentences.i: But whatever I hear, sitting here in our own halls, as is proper, you shall learn, and I will hide nothing from you.
sentences.n: μεγάροισι is a dative plural in -οισι, ‘in the halls’. πεύθομαι, ‘I learn by inquiry, hear tell’, contrasts with firsthand knowledge. ἣ θέμις ἐστί, ‘as is right, as custom allows’, is a formulaic aside. δαήσεαι, future middle from the same root as δαΐφρων, is ‘you shall learn’; κεύσω is future of κεύθω, ‘hide, conceal’.

sentences.t:
εὖ μὲν Μυρμιδόνας φάσ’ ἐλθέμεν ἐγχεσιμώρους,
οὓς ἄγ’ Ἀχιλλῆος μεγαθύμου φαίδιμος υἱός,
εὖ δὲ Φιλοκτήτην, Ποιάντιον ἀγλαὸν υἱόν.
sentences.l:
Well, they say, the Myrmidons, spear-wielding, came home,
whom led the glorious son of great-hearted Achilles,
and well Philoctetes, Poias' splendid son.
sentences.i: They say that the spear-wielding Myrmidons came home safely, led by the glorious son of great-hearted Achilles, and that Philoctetes, the splendid son of Poias, came home safely too.
sentences.n: ἐγχεσιμώρους, ‘spear-wielding, spear-mad’, is a stock epithet of the Myrmidons, Achilles' own troops. Ἀχιλλῆος μεγαθύμου φαίδιμος υἱός, ‘the glorious son of great-hearted Achilles’, is a periphrasis for Neoptolemus, left unnamed. Philoctetes, son of Poias, was the archer left wounded on Lemnos and later fetched to help take Troy.

sentences.t:
πάντας δ’ Ἰδομενεὺς Κρήτην εἰσήγαγ’ ἑταίρους,
οἳ φύγον ἐκ πολέμου, πόντος δέ οἱ οὔ τιν’ ἀπηύρα.
sentences.l:
and all his companions Idomeneus led into Crete,
as many as had fled from the war, and the sea took none of them from him.
sentences.i: And Idomeneus brought all his companions who had survived the war safely home to Crete, and the sea took none of them from him.
sentences.n: Idomeneus, king of Crete, led the Cretan contingent at Troy. εἰσήγαγ(ε), ‘led in, brought home’, is aorist of εἰσάγω. ἀπηύρα, ‘took away, robbed’, is an unaugmented aorist, with the dative οἱ, ‘from him’, meaning from Idomeneus' company.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδην δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ ἀκούετε, νόσφιν ἐόντες,
ὥς τ’ ἦλθ’, ὥς τ’ Αἴγισθος ἐμήσατο λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον.
sentences.l:
But of the son of Atreus even you yourselves have heard, being far off,
how he came, and how Aegisthus contrived his grievous destruction.
sentences.i: But of the son of Atreus, even you, far off as you were, have heard how he returned, and how Aegisthus contrived his grievous death.
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδην here names Agamemnon by the fixed periphrasis alone. νόσφιν ἐόντες, ‘being far off’, refers to Telemachus and his companions, who could not have witnessed these events. λυγρὸν ὄλεθρον, ‘grievous destruction’, echoes λυγρόν at 132, the same word now applied to one man's death.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι κεῖνος μὲν ἐπισμυγερῶς ἀπέτισεν·
sentences.l: but that man, indeed, paid for it most grievously;
sentences.i: But Aegisthus, at least, paid a bitter penalty for it;
sentences.n: ἐπισμυγερῶς, ‘most grievously, to his sorrow’, is a rare intensive adverb built on σμυγερός ‘woeful’ with the intensifying prefix ἐπι-. ἀπέτισεν, ‘paid the penalty, made requital’, is aorist of ἀποτίνω, the same root as the τίσασθαι/ἐτίσατο that recur through the rest of this part, in both Nestor's and Telemachus's speeches.

sentences.t:
ὡς ἀγαθὸν καὶ παῖδα καταφθιμένοιο λιπέσθαι
ἀνδρός, ἐπεὶ καὶ κεῖνος ἐτίσατο πατροφονῆα,
Αἴγισθον δολόμητιν, ὅ οἱ πατέρα κλυτὸν ἔκτα.
sentences.l:
How good a thing it is that even a son should be left behind by a man
who has perished, since that man too took vengeance on his father's slayer,
Aegisthus of guileful counsel, who had killed his famous father.
sentences.i: How good a thing it is that a dead man should leave a son behind, since that son too took vengeance on his father's slayer, Aegisthus of guileful counsel, who had killed his famous father.
sentences.n: ὡς ἀγαθόν, ‘how good a thing’, opens Nestor's general reflection, prompted by Orestes, whom he does not name here. καταφθιμένοιο, ‘having perished’, is a genitive participle with ἀνδρός. πατροφονῆα, ‘father-slayer’, stands in a line (197) that is not itself a repeat, though the same word appears in the earlier repeated line too; the following whole line, 198 (Αἴγισθον δολόμητιν, ὅ οἱ πατέρα κλυτὸν ἔκτα), is identical to the line already published at 1.300 (odyssey-003), and its English is kept the same there.

sentences.t:
καὶ σὺ φίλος, μάλα γάρ σ’ ὁρόω καλόν τε μέγαν τε,
ἄλκιμος ἔσσ’, ἵνα τίς σε καὶ ὀψιγόνων ἐὺ εἴπῃ.
sentences.l:
You too, friend — for very much I see you fine and tall —
be valiant, so that someone even of those born later may speak well of you.”
sentences.i: You too, my friend — for I see that you are very fine and tall — be brave, so that men born long after may speak well of you.”
sentences.n: This couplet is the same formula already published at 1.301–302 (odyssey-003), and its English is kept the same; the source's own printing of the line differs slightly in accent and comma from that occurrence (καὶ σὺ φίλος with no comma here, against καὶ σύ, φίλος there), an ordinary punctuation variant between the two printings of the formula, not a difference in wording, so the same English stands. ἄλκιμος ἔσσ(ο) is an aorist imperative, ‘be valiant’. ὀψιγόνων, ‘those born later’, means posterity. Nestor turns from Orestes' example to press the same course on Telemachus, and closes his speech here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This reply-formula is identical to the line already published at 1.388 (odyssey-004), and its English is kept the same. πεπνυμένος, ‘prudent’, is Telemachus's standing epithet; ἀντίον ηὔδα, ‘spoke face to face’, marks a direct, weighty reply rather than the plain verb ἠμείβετο.

sentences.t:
ὦ Νέστορ Νηληϊάδη, μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν,
καὶ λίην κεῖνος μὲν ἐτίσατο, καί οἱ Ἀχαιοὶ
οἴσουσι κλέος εὐρὺ καὶ ἐσσομένοισι πυθέσθαι·
sentences.i: “Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Achaeans, that man indeed took full vengeance, and the Achaeans will carry his wide fame even to generations yet to come;
sentences.n: The vocative line reuses the wording already fixed for the same line at 3.79 (odyssey-009). καὶ λίην, ‘yes, very much so’, is emphatic agreement with Nestor's words. κεῖνος, ‘that man’, is still unnamed Orestes. ἐσσομένοισι, ‘those who are to be’, a future participle used as a noun, is ‘future generations’; πυθέσθαι, ‘to hear of’, is epexegetic with κλέος.

sentences.t:
αἲ γὰρ ἐμοὶ τοσσήνδε θεοὶ δύναμιν περιθεῖεν,
τίσασθαι μνηστῆρας ὑπερβασίης ἀλεγεινῆς,
οἵ τέ μοι ὑβρίζοντες ἀτάσθαλα μηχανόωνται.
sentences.l:
Would that on me so great a power the gods might set about,
to take vengeance on the suitors for their grievous transgression,
who, insolent toward me, contrive wanton deeds.
sentences.i: If only the gods would grant me so much power, to punish the suitors for their grievous outrage, who insult me and plot their reckless deeds.
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ with the optative περιθεῖεν is a wish, ‘would that …’. τοσσήνδε δύναμιν, ‘so great a power’, sets up the infinitive τίσασθαι, ‘to punish, exact requital’. ἀτάσθαλα, ‘wanton, reckless deeds’, is the adjective behind the table's fixed noun ἀτασθαλίαι, ‘wanton-follies’, here used substantively.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὔ μοι τοιοῦτον ἐπέκλωσαν θεοὶ ὄλβον,
πατρί τ’ ἐμῷ καὶ ἐμοί·
sentences.l:
But not such fortune for me have the gods spun,
both for my father and for me;
sentences.i: But the gods have not spun out such good fortune for me, nor for my father either;
sentences.n: ἐπέκλωσαν, ‘spun’, is the same fate-spinning verb ἐπικλώθω already used (as the middle ἐπεκλώσαντο) at 1.17, though that is not itself a house-table entry. ὄλβον, ‘prosperity, good fortune’, is its object; πατρί τ’ ἐμῷ καὶ ἐμοί, ‘for my father and for me’, extends the lack of fortune to Odysseus as well as Telemachus.

sentences.t: νῦν δὲ χρὴ τετλάμεν ἔμπης.
sentences.l: but now it is necessary to endure nonetheless.”
sentences.i: but for now we must simply endure it.”
sentences.n: χρή with the infinitive τετλάμεν (perfect infinitive of τλῆναι, ‘to endure’) states a plain necessity. ἔμπης, ‘nonetheless, all the same’, concedes the wish just voiced. The full stop closes a complete sentence, and Telemachus's speech itself ends here too: the source's next line opens a fresh paragraph with the reply-formula τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ (Odyssey 3.210, in the next part), so this is not direct discourse running on but a new speech beginning after a narrator's frame — the closing quotation mark belongs here.
